paragraphs: The paper develops a way to combine astronomical measurements that describe light at very different spectral resolutions. Spectroscopy provides one kind of observation, while photometry provides another. The model connects them through a shared, unobserved spectral energy distribution: the underlying pattern of radiation that is intended to explain both sources of data.

A Gaussian process supplies a flexible, nonparametric prior over that distribution. This lets the model represent variation without committing to a fixed parametric shape. The construction also admits a physically interpretable decomposition and keeps inference tractable. Those properties matter together: the representation can accommodate varied spectra while supporting both interpretation and computation.

The application is predicting a quasar’s redshift from photometric observations in five bands. The output is a distribution over redshift, making uncertainty part of the prediction itself. The reported findings show that combining information across resolutions through a Bayesian model can produce accurate predictions with well-characterized uncertainty.
neurips-2015-a-gaussian-process-model-of.tldr: A Bayesian model connects spectroscopy and photometry through a shared latent spectrum to predict quasar redshifts with characterized uncertainty.

paragraphs: Traditional submodular cover uses sets, where an element is either selected or absent. This paper extends the problem to integer-valued decisions, allowing each coordinate to represent an amount. It retains a diminishing-returns property: additional increments provide less benefit as the existing allocation grows. This formulation captures machine learning scenarios that ordinary set functions cannot express.

The authors develop a bicriteria approximation algorithm, giving guarantees on both solution quality and constraint satisfaction. It returns a solution within a logarithmic approximation factor while meeting the constraints to the requested accuracy. These are approximation guarantees, so the result does not require finding an exact optimum.

The running time is roughly O(n log(nr) log r), with n coordinates and maximum coordinate value r. Its dependence on r is exponentially better than that of naive reductions. Experiments on real and artificial datasets report comparable solution quality to naive algorithms, with runtime improvements of several orders of magnitude. The contribution therefore joins a broader decision model with a substantially more efficient way to solve it approximately.
neurips-2015-a-generalization-of-submodu.tldr: The paper extends submodular cover to integer allocations and gives an approximation algorithm with much better dependence on allocation size.

paragraphs: The paper treats information collection as a market in which participants arrive in sequence and can sell what they know. Their contributions may be individual data points or more sophisticated information. The mechanism draws on prediction-market principles to connect participation with improving future predictions on a test set.

The participation incentive is conditional on participants’ beliefs. They are motivated to contribute when they believe their data are representative or their information will improve predictions. The mechanism operates with a bounded budget and minimizes generalization error for Bregman divergence losses. This connects the economic problem of eliciting information with a specified family of prediction objectives.

The authors also modify the mechanism to protect participants’ information. At any given time, its current prices and predictions reveal almost no information about any single participant, while the combined information remains accurately aggregated. The result links useful collective prediction with limited individual disclosure. Its privacy statement concerns what the current market outputs reveal, rather than claiming that the mechanism exposes no information whatsoever.
neurips-2015-a-market-framework-for-elic.tldr: A bounded-budget prediction market elicits useful information and can be modified to limit what its outputs reveal about individual participants.

paragraphs: Graph kernels compare graphs through their constituent structures. This paper introduces smoothing that accounts for similarity between those structures, making comparisons less brittle when edges or labels are noisy. The framework is general enough to produce smoothed versions of several existing graph kernels, rather than supplying only one isolated comparison rule.

The approach draws inspiration from smoothing methods in natural language processing. Its technical challenge is extending ideas used for strings to graph substructures whose relationships are interdependent. The authors also discuss adaptations of the Pitman–Yor process for structured objects. These constructions address diagonal dominance, where self-similarities overwhelm comparisons between different graphs, while retaining sensitivity to structural resemblance.

Experiments show improvements over the unsmoothed versions and statistically significant classification gains over several other graph kernels considered in the evaluation. Runtime is reported as competitive. Together, these findings support smoothing as a practical way to improve graph comparison, especially when small structural or labeling changes would otherwise obscure useful similarities.
neurips-2015-a-structural-smoothing-fram.tldr: Structure-aware smoothing improves graph kernels’ robustness and delivers reported classification gains with competitive runtime.

paragraphs: A bandit agent learns by choosing actions and observing rewards. This paper distinguishes that active experimentation from passively observing which actions occurred and what followed. When an unmeasured variable affects both the action and its outcome, the relationships found through observation generally differ from those obtained through intervention.

The authors show that this distinction changes what a bandit agent should optimize. Traditional algorithms implicitly pursue rewards using the experimental distribution. The paper argues that this is not always the best strategy: in certain classes of problems with unobserved confounding, achieving low regret requires both observational and experimental quantities. The claim concerns those settings, rather than every bandit problem.

The proposed optimization metric explicitly combines the two distributions, and the authors illustrate benefits over traditional algorithms. The contribution is therefore conceptual as well as algorithmic. It identifies circumstances in which information about naturally occurring actions remains relevant even for an agent that can actively experiment, and incorporates that information into the objective guiding its decisions.
neurips-2015-bandits-with-unobserved-con.tldr: In certain confounded bandit settings, low-regret decisions require an objective that combines observational and experimental information.

paragraphs: Distributed learning divides work among machines, but those machines still need to exchange information to solve a shared problem. This paper studies fundamental limits on that communication for convex learning and optimization. Its analysis varies both the information available locally and the kinds of objective functions being optimized.

The results separate settings where existing algorithms already attain the best possible worst-case communication behavior from settings where further improvement remains possible. Worst-case optimality means that no method covered by the corresponding assumptions can uniformly avoid the identified difficulty. This distinction helps determine whether reducing communication calls for a better algorithm or stronger assumptions about the problem.

A central finding concerns similarity between machines’ local objectives. Without such similarity, many communication rounds may be necessary even when local computation is unlimited. Similarity may arise from statistically similar data or other structure. The result shows why additional processing power alone may not remove the coordination bottleneck: information held across machines can still need repeated exchange.
neurips-2015-communication-complexity-of.tldr: The paper identifies communication limits in distributed convex optimization, showing that dissimilar local objectives can require many rounds despite unlimited local computation.

paragraphs: Some neural networks predict targets with enormous dimensionality even though only a few target entries are nonzero. Sparsity in the target does not automatically make training cheap, because the predicted output is typically dense. Computing that output, updating its weight matrix, and propagating gradients can each incur costs proportional to the output dimension D times the hidden dimension d.

The paper develops an algorithm that avoids explicitly forming the D-dimensional output. For a family of losses including squared error and spherical softmax, it computes the exact loss, output-weight update, and gradient for earlier layers in O(d²) work per example instead of O(Dd). Exactness is a central feature, and the supported loss family is an essential qualification.

The stated speedup for this computational component is D divided by 4d, reaching about two orders of magnitude for typical dimensions discussed in the abstract. This applies to a part of training that often dominates these architectures. It does not by itself state the same speedup for every operation in the complete network.
neurips-2015-efficient-exact-gradient-up.tldr: For a specified family of losses, exact training computations with huge sparse targets can avoid constructing the output and cost O(d²) per example.

paragraphs: The paper addresses answering simple questions about images through contributions to both modeling and data creation. Its model combines neural networks with visual semantic embeddings to predict answers. It does so without intermediate object-detection or image-segmentation stages, bringing visual and language information into the answer-prediction process directly.

On an existing image question-answering dataset, the authors report performance 1.8 times better than the only previously published results available for that dataset. This is a comparison within the stated evaluation, rather than a claim about all visual reasoning tasks. It supports the usefulness of the proposed modeling approach for the simple image questions studied.

The second contribution is an algorithm that converts image descriptions into question-answer pairs. Because descriptions are widely available, this provides a route to expanding the data used for the task. The resulting dataset is an order of magnitude larger and has more evenly distributed answers. The authors also provide baseline results, establishing reference performance for evaluating models on the new collection.
neurips-2015-exploring-models-and-data-f.tldr: The paper introduces a neural image question-answering model and generates a larger, more answer-balanced dataset from image descriptions.

paragraphs: The paper studies how quickly learning players approach efficient outcomes and coarse correlated equilibria in multiplayer normal-form games. It identifies classes of regularized learning algorithms with a form of recency bias. Their key advantage appears when every player uses an algorithm from the analyzed class, so the interacting learners have compatible behavior.

Under that condition, individual regret decays at O(T^(-3/4)), while the sum of players’ utilities approaches an approximate optimum at O(T^(-1)). Both improve on the O(T^(-1/2)) worst-case rates used for comparison. The efficiency claim remains approximate: faster convergence does not turn the destination into an exact optimum.

The authors also give a black-box reduction that preserves the faster rates against algorithms in the class while achieving a rate of roughly O(T^(-1/2)), up to logarithmic factors, against an adversary. This connects favorable interaction with protection against less predictable opponents. The analysis extends beyond earlier results restricted to particular algorithms in two-player zero-sum games, covering a broader multiplayer setting.
neurips-2015-fast-convergence-of-regular.tldr: Certain regularized learners converge faster when all players use the analyzed class, while a reduction retains adversarial regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Multi-label learning assigns several possible labels to each example. This paper builds a Bayesian model in which a label vector arises from a weighted combination of topics, each representing a distribution over labels. The topic weights form a low-dimensional embedding and depend on the example’s observed features.

A Bernoulli–Poisson link connects that topic representation to individual binary labels. This construction makes computational cost scale with the number of positive entries in the label matrix. That matters when the matrix is enormous but sparse: the model’s computation can follow the relatively small collection of present labels rather than treating every possible label entry equally.

A data-augmentation strategy gives the model full local conjugacy, enabling efficient Gibbs sampling and an expectation-maximization inference algorithm. At prediction time, label vectors can be predicted in closed form without separately inferring their embeddings. The authors report benchmark comparisons with existing methods. The abstract’s central scalability claims concern exploiting sparse positive labels and avoiding an additional embedding-inference step during prediction.
neurips-2015-large-scale-bayesian-multi-.tldr: A Bayesian topic-based label model exploits sparse positive labels for scalable learning and supports closed-form test-time prediction.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover the structure of a probabilistic graphical model without assuming a particular parametric distribution. Restrictive distributional choices can limit where structure-learning methods apply. The authors instead use an infinite-dimensional exponential family represented through a reproducing kernel Hilbert space and its kernel.

This flexibility brings a computational difficulty: evaluating the normalizing constant needed to turn an unnormalized density into a probability distribution. The proposed procedure avoids that calculation by minimizing a penalized score-matching objective. The authors show that existing group lasso solvers can efficiently minimize the resulting objective, connecting the flexible statistical model to available optimization machinery.

The theoretical result establishes recovery of the graph structure with high probability under conditions described as mild in the abstract. It is therefore a conditional recovery guarantee, not a promise for every distribution or dataset. Simulations illustrate recovery of the true graph without knowing the data-generating process. Together, the results support structure learning with fewer commitments to a fixed parametric form.
neurips-2015-learning-structured-densiti.tldr: Kernel-based exponential families and penalized score matching enable nonparametric graph-structure learning with conditional high-probability recovery guarantees.

paragraphs: The Mind the Gap Model addresses feature selection and extraction with interpretability built into the model itself. The aim is to identify dimensions that people can distinguish and use when exploring data. Its output is a global set of such dimensions, providing a view of the dataset that can support further investigation and hypothesis generation.

The central design choice is to include interpretability criteria directly in modeling. This allows parameters related to interpretability to be optimized during learning and lets the model report the resulting dimensions directly. Interpretability therefore shapes the representation being learned, making the selected or extracted features part of the model’s intended explanatory output.

The authors demonstrate distinguishing features in datasets covering animals, recipe ingredients, and disease co-occurrence. They report maintained or improved performance relative to related approaches and conduct a study with domain experts showing usefulness for dataset exploration. These findings connect the model’s design to both computational performance and human use, supporting its role as an exploratory tool.
neurips-2015-mind-the-gap-a-generative-a.tldr: Mind the Gap builds interpretability into feature learning and reports useful distinguishing dimensions for expert-guided data exploration.

paragraphs: Mixing time describes how long a Markov chain takes to approach its equilibrium behavior. This paper estimates it from one finite observed trajectory of a finite, reversible, ergodic chain. The procedure produces a fully data-dependent interval with a prescribed confidence level, without requiring knowledge of the chain’s parameters.

The interval is constructed around the closely related relaxation time. Its width shrinks toward zero at approximately an inverse-square-root rate in the trajectory length. Unlike approaches that give only a point estimate, this supplies an explicit uncertainty interval. It also avoids requiring a mechanism that resets the chain or additional prior information about it.

The authors establish upper and lower sample requirements for achieving constant-factor multiplicative accuracy. Without further restrictions on the chain, the lower bounds require observing each state on average at least on the order of the relaxation time. This identifies a fundamental data requirement, rather than merely a weakness of the proposed estimator, and explains why a short trajectory may be insufficient for accurate mixing-time estimation.
neurips-2015-mixing-time-estimation-in-r.tldr: A single trajectory yields a confidence interval for a reversible ergodic chain’s mixing time, with guarantees on accuracy and necessary sample coverage.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a ranking through a sequence of pairwise comparisons. It assumes that rankings follow a Plackett–Luce distribution. The learner can query comparisons between alternatives over time and uses those observations to predict either the most probable complete ranking or the top alternative reliably.

The proposed approach constructs a substitute distribution over rankings using a sorting procedure. Its key theoretical property is that its pairwise comparison probabilities exactly match those of the assumed Plackett–Luce distribution. This connects the constructed ranking representation to the information the learner actually observes. Matching these pairwise probabilities is the stated result; it does not assert that the two complete ranking distributions are identical.

The authors provide formal analyses of performance and computational complexity, together with initial experimental studies. The contribution offers a bridge between online comparison queries and ranking prediction through a mathematically justified surrogate. Its interpretation depends on the Plackett–Luce assumption, which specifies the relationship between the observed pairwise outcomes and the ranking the learner seeks.
neurips-2015-online-rank-elicitation-for.tldr: Under a Plackett–Luce model, a sorting-based surrogate with matching pairwise probabilities supports online ranking prediction from comparison queries.

paragraphs: Principal differences analysis seeks an interpretable description of how two high-dimensional distributions differ. It searches for a projection that makes their resulting one-dimensional populations as different as possible, measured using Wasserstein divergence. The output therefore identifies a direction along which the distributions’ differences become especially visible.

The framework relies on the Cramér–Wold device and does not require assumptions about the distributions’ forms or the nature of their differences. A sparse version identifies features responsible for the separation, making the projection easier to interpret. The authors provide algorithms for the original minimax problem and a semidefinite relaxation, along with some convergence results.

An application uses single-cell RNA sequencing to characterize differences between cell populations in the somatosensory cortex and hippocampus. This illustrates how the method can connect distributional comparison with feature-level interpretation in complex data. The broader framework also permits choices beyond Wasserstein divergence, so its organizing idea is the search for informative projected differences rather than dependence on only one comparison measure.
neurips-2015-principal-differences-analy.tldr: Principal differences analysis finds projections that expose distributional differences, with a sparse variant highlighting the features involved.

paragraphs: A line search chooses how far an optimization algorithm should move along a proposed direction. With exact information, it can make firm decisions about which step lengths are acceptable. Stochastic gradients complicate this process because noisy observations do not support the same strict sequence of decisions about narrowing the search.

The paper builds a probabilistic version by combining deterministic line-search structure with ideas from Bayesian optimization. A Gaussian process models the objective along the one-dimensional search direction. The algorithm tracks probabilistic beliefs about the Wolfe conditions, which guide whether a step provides suitable descent. Uncertainty is therefore included in evaluating candidate steps.

The method has low computational cost and no user-controlled parameters. Experiments show that it effectively removes the need to specify a learning rate for stochastic gradient descent. This finding supports an automated way to choose step sizes in the evaluated settings. The contribution is a concrete decision procedure for noisy line searches, supported by empirical evidence that it can reduce learning-rate tuning.
neurips-2015-probabilistic-line-searches.tldr: A Gaussian-process line search uses probabilistic descent conditions to automate stochastic gradient step sizes with little computational overhead.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo samples continuous distributions by simulating motion governed by an energy function. Non-smooth functions can make that simulated motion difficult to compute and harm sampling performance. This paper addresses the problem by drawing inspiration from physical reflection and refraction, where motion changes when a trajectory crosses an interface.

The authors modify the leapfrog discretization for piecewise continuous energies. The method detects where a simulated trajectory encounters a discontinuity and adjusts momentum through reflection or refraction to account for the energy change. Handling those encounters explicitly gives the simulation a way to respond to boundaries that its usual smooth-motion calculations do not accommodate well.

The authors prove preservation of the correct stationary distribution when the boundaries are affine. That boundary condition is part of the theoretical guarantee. Experiments show improved performance over traditional Hamiltonian Monte Carlo through fewer rejected samples. The paper thus combines a boundary-aware integration method with a correctness result for the stated setting and empirical evidence of improved sampling behavior.
neurips-2015-reflection-refraction-and-h.tldr: Reflecting or refracting momentum at energy discontinuities improves HMC empirically and preserves the target stationary distribution for affine boundaries.

paragraphs: Choosing a regularization parameter can strongly affect a model’s generalization performance. Cross-validation helps compare choices, but a grid of evaluated values leaves a question unanswered: could an untested value perform substantially better? This paper develops a way to quantify that uncertainty across an entire parameter range.

The framework computes lower bounds on cross-validation error as a function of the regularization parameter. These bounds form a regularization path describing how low the error could be throughout the range. Comparing them with the best evaluated solution gives a theoretical approximation guarantee on the remaining possible improvement, making the quality of the current search assessable.

Numerical experiments show that parameter selection with this kind of guarantee is possible at reasonable computational cost. The guarantee concerns proximity to the best cross-validation error over the specified range, rather than direct certification of future prediction error. The contribution makes parameter tuning more principled by connecting evaluated candidates to bounds on what untested choices could achieve.
neurips-2015-regularization-path-of-cros.tldr: Lower bounds across the regularization range certify how close the best tested parameter is to the smallest possible cross-validation error.

paragraphs: Metric learning changes the representation of data so that distances become more useful for prediction. This paper asks how much supervised data is needed to learn a Mahalanobis distance metric reliably. It gives PAC-style sample-complexity rates, connecting the amount of training information to guarantees about learned performance.

Without assumptions on the underlying data distribution, matching upper and lower bounds show dependence on the representation dimension. The lower bound makes this more than a weakness of one particular method. When the distribution has exploitable structure, however, the authors derive rates tied to a specific notion of intrinsic dataset complexity, relaxing the dependence on the full representation dimension.

The paper also studies adding a simple norm-based regularizer to the learning objective. Theory and experiments show that this can help the learner adapt to intrinsic complexity and improve generalization. The result partly explains previously observed benefits of related regularization methods. It also clarifies why the ambient number of features need not be the only useful measure of learning difficulty.
neurips-2015-sample-complexity-of-learni.tldr: Metric-learning sample bounds depend on representation dimension in general, while distributional structure and norm regularization can enable adaptation to intrinsic complexity.

paragraphs: The paper develops stochastic optimal control from a learned probabilistic model of system dynamics. Using the path-integral approach, it derives iterative control laws analytically without requiring a policy parameterization in advance. Uncertainty in the learned dynamics is part of the representation used to construct the controller.

Its computation proceeds through a forward-backward sweep. This distinguishes it from path-integral methods that use forward sampling to obtain open-loop controls. The authors report needing significantly less sampled data than approaches in that family that depend on extensive simulation from dynamics models or repeated model-free trials on physical systems.

The learned controllers can also be generalized to new tasks without resampling through compositionality in the linearly solvable optimal-control framework. That framework provides the basis for the transfer claim. Experiments on three systems, including comparisons with state-of-the-art model-based methods, demonstrate the proposed method’s efficiency and generalizability. The contribution combines analytical controller construction, a probabilistic dynamics model, and a way to reuse learned control information across tasks.
neurips-2015-sample-efficient-path-integ.tldr: A probabilistic path-integral control method derives analytical controllers with fewer samples and supports task reuse through linearly solvable control compositionality.

paragraphs: Kernel component methods uncover nonlinear structure but can become difficult to use on very large datasets. Random-feature approximations offer one route to reducing computation, yet high-quality solutions can require a number of features comparable to the number of observations. At millions of observations, that requirement remains a substantial scaling obstacle.

The paper proposes an efficient, memory-friendly algorithm based on doubly stochastic gradients for kernel PCA, CCA, and SVD. It also avoids explicit orthogonalization, a computational requirement the abstract identifies as infeasible at large scale. The design therefore addresses both the representation burden and a costly operation associated with learning component subspaces.

Despite the nonconvex objectives, the authors establish convergence to the global optimum at a rate of roughly 1/t, up to logarithmic factors, including for the leading k-dimensional eigensubspace. This is a guarantee for the analyzed method and problems. Experiments on large synthetic and real datasets demonstrate effectiveness and scalability, linking the theoretical result to the practical goal of expanding nonlinear component analysis.
neurips-2015-scale-up-nonlinear-componen.tldr: Doubly stochastic gradients scale kernel component analysis while avoiding explicit orthogonalization and providing global-convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering an unknown vector from measurements that square the magnitude of its inner products with known vectors. These quadratic measurements lead to a nonconvex recovery problem. For the random, unstructured systems studied, the authors prove exact recovery from a number of equations proportional to the number of variables, with time proportional to reading and evaluating the data.

The algorithm begins with a spectral estimate and then minimizes a nonconvex objective. Its distinguishing feature is adaptive filtering during both initialization and descent. Terms with excessive influence are discarded, preventing them from dominating the initial guess or subsequent search directions. The authors interpret these selection rules as variance reduction, producing tighter initialization and more robust updates.

The method also achieves near-optimal statistical accuracy when measurements contain noise. Empirically, its computational cost is reported as about four times that of a same-sized least-squares problem. That comparison supports the title’s practical message for the studied systems, while the exact-recovery and noisy-data claims describe different measurement settings.
neurips-2015-solving-random-quadratic-sy.tldr: Adaptive filtering enables efficient recovery in the studied random quadratic systems, with exact noiseless recovery and near-optimal accuracy under noise.

paragraphs: Dimensionality reduction seeks a compact representation that retains useful information about data. This paper explores space-time as the representation used for that task. Drawing on a concept from physics, it asks whether changing the geometry of the embedding can preserve relationships that are harder to express in ordinary Euclidean space.

The authors introduce basic definitions and discuss counterintuitive properties of this representation. They also give theoretical propositions showing that space-time offers greater representational power than Euclidean space. This theoretical contribution provides a reason to consider a different embedding geometry when the relationships in a dataset are not well captured by the usual spatial representation.

The paper applies the idea to manifold learning with an emphasis on preserving local information. Empirical results on non-metric datasets show that space-time embeddings can retain more information. The stated finding is specific to those evaluations, rather than a universal advantage for every dataset. Together, the theory and experiments connect the choice of representation with how much local structure dimensionality reduction can preserve.
neurips-2015-space-time-local-embeddings.tldr: Space-time embeddings offer greater representational power than Euclidean space and preserve more information in the reported non-metric-data experiments.

paragraphs: Persistence diagrams summarize topological features in data through persistent homology. The paper asks how to perform principled statistical computations with these diagrams. It follows an approach inspired by embedding probability distributions into reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, where kernel-based methods provide a common mathematical setting for comparing distributions.

A positive definite kernel for persistence diagrams had already connected these objects to learning methods such as support vector machines. The authors identify a remaining theoretical gap: properties needed to use that connection for probability-distribution embeddings had not been established. They address it by proving universality for a variant of the existing kernel, supplying a stronger mathematical foundation for statistical use.

The paper demonstrates the resulting approach through two-sample hypothesis testing on synthetic and real-world data. Such testing asks whether two collections are consistent with the same underlying distribution. The contribution therefore moves beyond using topological summaries as inputs to prediction: it supports statistical comparison of populations represented by persistence diagrams and demonstrates that use empirically.
neurips-2015-statistical-topological-dat.tldr: A universality proof for a persistence-diagram kernel supports principled distribution embeddings and effective two-sample testing.

paragraphs: The paper studies partitioning items linked by shared associations, represented as a hypergraph or an item-topic bipartite graph. Its objective is to minimize the largest number of topics covered by any partition. This makes the most heavily burdened part the focus, with applications including clustering information objects and balancing computational loads.

The setting is streaming: items arrive one at a time, and each assignment must be made immediately and cannot be reversed. Memory is limited to at most a linear function of the number of partitions. These requirements make scalability part of the problem definition, ruling out reliance on retaining and repeatedly reorganizing the full input.

The authors analyze a greedy assignment strategy and prove that it recovers a hidden co-clustering under a stated set of recovery conditions. The guarantee is conditional, rather than applying to arbitrary streams. An extensive empirical evaluation also finds superior performance over the alternatives considered. The results show how a simple assignment rule can combine strict streaming constraints with useful structural recovery.
neurips-2015-streaming-min-max-hypergrap.tldr: A memory-efficient greedy streaming rule partitions hypergraph items and recovers hidden co-clustering under specified conditions.
